The description seems to track the sea's changing aspect as a rhythmic alternation of swelling and tightening, so that the same water appears by turns immense and confined, with the final movement returning it to openness.

AGENTS: The sea itself ('il mare') is the sole grammatical and thematic agent of the passage — it expands, contracts, and expands again; any human observer is implied rather than named (UNKNOWN whether a narrator or character watches it).

You are assisting with a scholarly experiment in structural literary analysis.

TASK: Do not write any new text. The specification below was written for a writing experiment. It describes one formal pattern, abstracted from one existing literary passage (which is not shown) and from a critical reading of that passage. Reconstruct, as far as the specification allows, what the source passage contained: what it described or narrated, who or what acted in it, and which of its words or phrases the specification seems to echo. Where the specification gives you no ground for a reconstruction, write UNKNOWN. You need not identify the work; name it only if you recognise it.

SPECIFICATION:
[C-P5-01] (MUST) from P_5: Mare duality — alternating contraction/dilation lexicon, full arc
  Specification: Two opposed lexical fields alternate over the single referent 'il mare': one of expansion, one of constriction. The words of both fields are yours to choose; none are supplied. The passage runs the full arc expansion -> constriction -> re-expansion. Audited by locating the two fields in the text and checking the arc order.

Answer in a few sentences, naming the author and the title of the work if you know them, or saying that you do not.

The specification points to an Italian prose passage (P_5) whose single governing subject is "il mare" — the sea — described through two antithetical registers applied to the same referent: one of opening out (breadth, swelling, widening, the horizon dilating, the sea spreading or growing immense) and one of closing in (narrowing, shrinking, tightening, the sea drawing together, pressed or hemmed into a strait or basin). The passage evidently traces a three-beat movement: the sea first appears vast and dilated, then contracts or is constricted, then opens out again — a rhythm that could be literal (a coastline narrowing into a strait and then releasing into open water, or a tide/swell breathing in and out) or perceptual (the sea seen from a moving vantage, a boat or a shore, alternately widening and closing around the observer).

Beyond this, the specification supplies no content: it explicitly withholds the actual vocabulary of both fields, so the particular words the source used (and therefore which phrases the spec "echoes") are UNKNOWN. The only phrase quoted is "il mare" itself, which indicates the source is in Italian and that the sea is the grammatical and thematic subject throughout. Any human actors, narrator, setting, plot action, or figurative frame (e.g. the sea as breath, as living body, as mirror) are UNKNOWN.

I do not recognise the specific work or author with any confidence; the Italian wording and the breathing-sea motif are suggestive of writers such as Calvino, Morante, or D'Annunzio, but I cannot identify it.
